Research dating back to the 1970s had made partial progress, but AlphaFold, built on models trained on experimentally determined structures and sequence data, produced accurate models in minutes to hours. The second generation dominated the blind competition CASP in 2020, and the third generation, in 2024, expanded its scope to predicting interactions involving DNA, RNA, and candidate drugs. That same year, Jumper and CEO Demis Hassabis shared half of the Nobel Prize in Chemistry.

The team's dissolution coincides with bigger changes at DeepMind. Google announced on Wednesday that Hassabis is stepping down as DeepMind CEO to become Alphabet's chief scientist. His decision to release AlphaFold for free reportedly brought prestige but little direct revenue, and is said to have caused friction inside Google.

John Moult, a computational biologist at the University of Maryland who co-founded CASP, said back in 2020 that AlphaFold had already “largely solved” the structure-prediction problem. He says it's “not surprising” that DeepMind is now moving on. “They judged it a good problem because you can show success or failure cleanly.” From DeepMind's side, he says, the thinking is: “We did it, so what's the next mission?”

AlphaFold proved far more useful outside of CASP. Protein misfolding is tied to conditions like Alzheimer's disease and cystic fibrosis. Researchers have used the publicly available prediction data for everything from malaria vaccine research to breeding hardier crops.

Still, “largely solved” applies to a specific benchmark, not to structural biology as a whole. Many proteins work as parts of larger molecular machines and shift between multiple shapes while functioning. Predicting those changes, or figuring out how molecules will bind, remains difficult. “There's a whole list of these problems still sitting there, and they're definitely not all solved,” Moult says.

Debora Marks, a computational biologist at Harvard Medical School who pioneered the approach underlying AlphaFold, also said DeepMind's decision wasn't surprising. “I would have done the same thing. Why keep going once you've already finished?” DeepMind released AlphaFold3's inference code and model weights for academic research in 2024, and independent research teams have since released their own versions and extensions. Moult doesn't think the team's dissolution will slow that momentum. “It doesn't really affect the usefulness of what they did. Other people are doing it now.”

An AI system that automates cognitive testing of wild capuchin monkeys has arrived. CapuchinAI, built by researchers at Emory University and Georgia Tech, combines facial recognition with real-time touchscreen tasks, and the proof-of-concept paper appeared in the American Journal of Primatology. It's the first method for measuring wild primate cognition systematically, and at scale.

“Primate brains didn't evolve in a lab. They evolved in complex, highly competitive environments,” said Marcela Benítez, assistant professor of anthropology at Emory and the paper's lead author. “Yet studying primate cognition in the wild is rare, because measuring cognition in an unpredictable environment means you need to control the experiment.”

CapuchinAI puts a small, battery-powered computer inside field-research equipment. It recognizes which monkey has approached, displays a task tailored to that individual on a touchscreen, and automatically dispenses food when the task is solved correctly. In prototype trials at the Tabogo forest reserve in Costa Rica, the system identified individual capuchins with 97% accuracy. Wild capuchins quickly grew used to the equipment, learning that pressing the screen produced a reward.

blocks.cap: Thanks to machine vision, the model can switch tests from one individual to another instantly, letting several monkeys take part in a single session. Credit: the research team

blocks.x: The facial-recognition model was built by Jacob Abernethy, an associate professor at Georgia Tech, and Sai Lakshit Potluri, using the open-source YOLO framework. It was trained on six wild capuchins captured in high-resolution GoPro footage shot at Tabogo, with Emory and Georgia Tech undergraduates manually drawing facial bounding boxes and labeling names across thousands of photos and clips.

blocks.cap: Undergraduates drew bounding boxes around capuchin faces in field footage and labeled the individuals correctly. The monkeys pictured are Pelé, Pedro, Fio, and Pesto. Credit: Emory University

blocks.x: The next step fell to Federico Sánchez Vargas, an anthropology PhD student at Emory and the paper's first author. “The model recognized the six well, but there are about 100 capuchins in the field, and we didn't have high-resolution footage to train on for the rest.” He rewrote the model in Python so that, instead of identifying individuals, it simply flags “capuchin or not.” When a monkey approaches, a webcam automatically records, growing the training data on its own. A second script uses pygame to display stimuli on the screen, and pressing a blue square triggers a motor to dispense food. Both scripts run together on a Raspberry Pi about half the size of an iPhone, which lasts eight hours on a battery pack.

The enclosure to house the equipment was built in Benítez's garage. The team framed a box 51 centimeters tall out of pine boards, sealant, rubber strips, and plastic tubing, and 3D-printed the food dispenser at Emory's TechLab.

blocks.cap: Sánchez Vargas and Benítez were still tweaking the box they'd designed and built themselves until 11 p.m. the night before leaving for Costa Rica. Credit: Emory University

blocks.x: No one approached for the first two days in the field. On the third day, a male named Trompudo — meaning “big snout” — couldn't resist the smell of bananas, climbed onto the box, banged on the back, and hit the screen. A piece of dried banana dropped out. He touched it again, and another piece came out. “You could see it click: ‘oh, I just have to press the screen.’” Sixteen individuals touched the equipment during the pilot period. Some learned fast; others inspected the screen with their lips before kissing it; still others watched their friends first and approached only later.

The researchers are retraining the facial-recognition model on footage from the pilot period and preparing experiments across four domains: learning ability, impulse control, cognitive flexibility, and memory. The paper also released the code and the design for the low-cost equipment. “Our AI method doesn't replace human researchers in the field,” said Sánchez Vargas. “You still need observational data gathered by people on the ground.”

Two theoretical physicists, one a Nobel laureate. A math problem that had held them both for a decade was solved with the help of Anthropic's large language model Claude. It's a result in fundamental physics, and another sign that AI is changing how research gets done in some fields.

The setting is complex systems, specifically a phenomenon called jamming. “Jamming is a transition where a system in a fluid state suddenly and completely freezes while still disordered,” explains Francesco Zamponi, a physicist at Sapienza University of Rome. Imagine balls with no friction and no weight floating inside a zero-gravity box. Add more balls or inflate them, and space grows tight; at some critical density, each ball gets locked in place by its neighbors and the whole system stops moving. Freeze it slowly and you get a crystal, like oranges stacked at a market; compress it quickly and it freezes disordered, like a traffic jam.

blocks.cap: The authors of the original 2014 paper. From left: Giorgio Parisi, Patrick Charbonneau, Francesco Zamponi, Jorge Kurchan, and Pierfrancesco Urbani. Photo: Maurizio Perciballi

blocks.x: Jamming is also an instance of a much more general mathematical problem called constraint satisfaction. The position of each ball is a variable; the rule that no two balls can overlap is a constraint. That's why neuroscience and artificial intelligence use the same concept. In a neural network, synaptic weights are the variables, and the classifications it must learn are the constraints. “A neural network in a ‘liquid’ state adjusts its weights to meet every condition,” Zamponi says, “but once there's too much data, it hits a wall, turns ‘solid,’ and starts producing errors.”

In 2014, Giorgio Parisi and Zamponi, together with colleagues in the US and France, found a strange relationship in numerical calculations. Add together two parameters, a and b, tied to the distribution of contact forces and the scaling of the gaps between balls, and the sum was invariably 1. Both values are central to defining the packed structure, yet no matter how hard they tried, a formal proof of a + b = 1 never emerged. Parisi received half of the 2021 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Asking generative AI was Parisi's idea. It was a problem well-suited to handing off to a machine: the conjecture was clear, and there was even a numerical answer, but no analytical proof. The two chose Claude, judging its coding and mathematical reasoning to be stronger. Even so, they didn't ask for a proof right away. “We had it reproduce the numerical calculations our group made ten years ago first. Once it got the same results, we naturally asked the next question: ‘If a + b = 1, can you prove why?’”

The model's first attempt was broadly on the right track, but mixed in small mathematical errors that took multiple rounds of refining and checking. Still, Zamponi says the “core intuition” came from the AI. “We'd spent years searching for a complicated answer, something like a deeply hidden structural symmetry, and Claude showed us the answer was much simpler and right in front of us.” The new proof links Zamponi's team's infinite-dimensional theory with a framework built around the same time by Matthieu Wyart's team at EPFL, confirming that the two starting points lead to the same physical law.

Zamponi believes generative AI could become as important as the Industrial Revolution or the birth of the internet, maybe more so — a kind of “telescope for the mind” that accelerates the pace of research. On the other hand, he worries about a flood of shoddy pseudoscientific papers overwhelming peer review. The two researchers released the full transcript of their conversation with Claude alongside the paper. It was published in the Journal of Statistical Mechanics: Theory and Experiment.

AI chips are becoming increasingly programmable. Researchers at KAIST have built a device whose response characteristics can be programmed to handle data arriving at widely varying speeds. It cut prediction error for constantly changing data by up to 40 times, and is seen as a technology that could boost real-time AI performance in self-driving cars, robots, and wearable devices.

A team led by Chair Professor Choi Shin-hyun of the School of Electrical Engineering and the Graduate School of Semiconductor Systems Engineering developed a programmable dynamic memtransistor (PDM) that sets its time-response characteristics to multiple states and retains them, along with an integrated array of the devices. The paper was published in Nature Communications.

A memtransistor is a next-generation device that combines a memory's information-storage function with a transistor's computing function in one. The PDM processes data while retaining prior information, adjusting and maintaining its response characteristics to match the incoming data.

blocks.cap: The concept and operating principle of the programmable dynamic memtransistor (PDM), which processes time-series signals across multiple time scales. Conventional devices have a single fixed time response, limiting the range of time scales they can handle, but the PDM uses a dual-function gate structure to set response characteristics across multiple stages, from fast to slow, and retain them non-volatilely. Source: KAIST

blocks.x: Today's computers and smartphones need complex software processing to analyze data that changes over time, which comes with a heavy computational burden and high power consumption. Research has continued into letting hardware process data directly, but once a conventional device is fabricated, its response speed can't be changed.

The team got around this barrier by building a dual-layer structure inside the transistor: a charge-storage layer that accumulates and processes data, layered with an electron-trapping layer that non-volatilely tunes the response speed. Incoming data is processed in the charge-storage layer, while the electron-trapping layer adjusts, across multiple stages, how fast the device recovers back to its original state. In experiments, current recovery time was tunable across a roughly 5-fold range, and characteristic frequency across more than a 10-fold range.
In particular, in experiments predicting data where fast and slow changes were intertwined, the PDM cut error by up to 40 times compared with conventional devices that have a fixed response speed.

blocks.cap: The structure of a PDM array combining devices with different time-response characteristics, and its multi-timescale signal-processing performance. Each device is assigned a different time constant, from fast to slow response, so multiple time-series signals can be processed simultaneously. Source: KAIST

blocks.x: Accurate processing stays possible even when handwriting style or an object's movement speed changes, thanks to response characteristics tuned to the input's time scale. Once set, the response characteristics persist without a continuous external power supply, and the input data requires no separate preprocessing. The device is also compatible as-is with widely used commercial semiconductor process materials, which favors mass production and commercialization.

The team built a PDM array to predict complex data, matching the accuracy of existing software-based systems while using far less energy. Professor Choi Shin-hyun said, “This research demonstrates an AI chip whose response characteristics can be programmed to efficiently process data at different speeds,” adding that it “will become a key technology for boosting the performance of AI devices like self-driving cars, robots, and wearables while lowering their power consumption.”

When looking inside living cells, biology has long relied on fluorescent dyes. They work well, but they come at a cost: the cells being observed change, only a handful of structures can be seen at once, and measurement accuracy itself drops.

A team led by researchers at the University at Buffalo has come up with a way around these limits by pairing artificial intelligence with Raman spectroscopy. Ramanomics, an optical technique pioneered at Buffalo, measures a cell's biochemical makeup without disturbing it. Instead of fluorescent labels that latch onto specific components and glow under special lighting, it identifies structures by the unique biochemical fingerprint they carry.

blocks.cap: On the left, fluorescent labels are used to trace cell structures and collect biochemical data to create training examples for AI; on the right, AI distinguishes cell structures using only biochemical signals. Source: University at Buffalo, ACS Omega (2026)

blocks.x: “This interdisciplinary collaboration applying AI to Ramanomics is the first to show that organelles inside living cells can be identified non-invasively, without dye labeling,” said Dr. Paras N. Prasad, director of the Institute for Lasers, Photonics and Biophotonics at the University at Buffalo and SUNY Distinguished Professor. “It opens a path toward finding biological markers of disease, discovering new drugs, and more personalized medicine.”

“The moment you put a dye into a cell, you've introduced a foreign substance. That foreign substance disrupts the cell's natural behavior, which affects the very value you're trying to measure,” explained Dr. Varun Chandola, associate professor in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at the University at Buffalo. “Being able to look inside a cell without physically altering it is a major advance. Because it captures biology as it actually is, you get a more accurate picture of how the cell really works.”

The two are the lead researchers on a paper published in ACS Omega in June. The team captured biochemical “fingerprints” of four types of cell organelles using Raman spectroscopy, then used those fingerprints to train several machine learning models. Once trained, the AI could take in a new Raman measurement alone and pinpoint which part of the cell it came from. Among the models tested, a neural network performed best, correctly identifying organelles with about 90% accuracy.

With the step of formulating and introducing a dye gone, the workflow gets simpler, experimental artifacts drop, and measurement sensitivity rises. Watching cells for longer periods without disturbing them also opens new views into how diseases arise and spread, and how they respond to treatment. It also becomes easier to track the molecular changes tied to cancer or metabolic disease.

The team has now started work on attaching AI models to next-generation Raman imaging equipment that uses quantum light sources. “Right now, getting one reliable signal can take up to three minutes,” Chandola said, adding that “cutting that down to around a second would let us analyze far more cells at scale.” The team is also expanding the work toward using model outputs to distinguish cancer cells from normal ones.

Whether young people use AI for mental health issues is no longer the question. Health authorities say the real issue is whether the advice they receive is sound. A recent survey found that AI chatbot mental health consultations among teens and young adults rose 60% in a year, and the researchers who led it expect the trend to continue.

blocks.cap: Source: Pavel Danilyuk from Pexels

blocks.x: The study was led by Hao Yu, associate professor of population medicine at Harvard Medical School and the Harvard Pilgrim Health Care Institute, with 1,727 participants. While AI could fill the gap left by a shortage of mental health professionals, Yu said it is now time to examine whether the advice it gives helps or harms.

Asked what the survey found, Yu said: “In a similar study last year, one in eight young people aged 12 to 21 used AI for mental health issues. This year it was nearly one in five. That means close to 20% of young people in this country are seeking mental health advice from AI — a surge within a single year.” Usage rates were higher among older teens and young women.

“It may be surprising that most teens who use AI haven’t told either their parents or their doctor.” Yu said this is concerning because many AI models mix in inaccurate information and were never designed to give mental health advice in the first place. That’s why she urged parents and doctors to talk with children about their AI use — so they can notice if a child has a mental health issue, or help them tell accurate information from the misinformation scattered online.

The US health care system has a severe shortage of psychiatrists, especially child psychiatrists, and only half of people who need mental health treatment actually receive it. In that gap, AI has its own advantages. “AI is patient. It’s available any time, day or night, with no appointment needed. And it’s kind — it rarely gets harsh or irritated.” That is especially true in rural or remote areas with severe workforce shortages.

Quality is a separate issue. There have been cases where teens discussing mental health issues with AI led to tragedies, including suicide attempts. AI companies have promised to build in safeguards, but Yu pointed out there is no empirical evidence showing how well those promises are being kept. In this study, more than 90% of teens said the advice was useful, but whether it is truly helpful and accurate remains an empirical question still to be answered.

Most AI models are designed to be friendly and agreeable in order to keep users engaged, and young people are especially drawn in by that. Yu said development of AI trained specifically for therapeutic use should be accelerated, since it could help ease the shortage of child psychiatrists. Still, it is natural to worry about the quality and safety of such models, and some policymakers, such as those in Illinois, have already acted. In the end, she said, it comes down to patient safety.

A follow-up survey is also planned. Yu expects the rate to keep rising as long as AI remains part of young people’s daily lives and unmet mental health needs persist. There was one surprising finding: there was no significant difference between rural and urban areas, despite the digital divide and the far greater shortage of child psychiatrists in rural areas. If follow-up research confirms this, it could help offset the harm from workforce shortages — but only if those AI models meet the clinical standards for mental health advice.

Designing an effective antibody drug is a bit like finding the right key in a warehouse full of locks. There can be millions to billions of candidates, and only a tiny fraction recognize a disease target and bind to it tightly. Researchers at Boston University have introduced an antibody-specific AI framework that sharply narrows that search.

blocks.cap: An illustration of an antibody.

blocks.x: Most of an antibody is just scaffolding that holds the structure up. The information that determines what it recognizes and how tightly it binds is concentrated in six small loops called the complementarity-determining regions (CDRs). Dr. John Misasi explained it this way: “Think of an antibody like a screwdriver. It doesn't matter if it's long or short — what screw it fits depends on the shape of the tip. The CDR is that tip, and it decides which target the antibody recognizes.”

Instead of treating antibodies like ordinary proteins, the researchers redesigned the training process around antibody biology. They trained on more than 1.6 million naturally paired heavy- and light-chain antibody sequences, leaving the surrounding structure largely intact while deliberately masking up to half of the amino acids within the CDRs — forcing the model to repeatedly reconstruct the regions that matter most for binding.

The finished model has about 600 million parameters. On a dataset of more than 90,000 engineered antibody variants targeting six antigens, it boosted binding-affinity prediction by up to 27%, matching or beating much larger antibody language models across several benchmarks — while using less computing power.

Dr. Diane Joseph-McCarthy said, “We wanted to teach AI the biology that matters most, so we could give researchers better tools to discover, optimize, and ultimately design the next generation of antibody therapeutics.” Dr. Misasi added that narrowing millions of possibilities down to a few hundred promising ones saves enormous amounts of lab time, personnel, and cost. The paper was published on August 13 in Communications AI & Computing.

Google Research has extended its medical conversation AI, AMIE, to real-time video consultations. It now reads not just what patients describe in words, but what they show in front of the camera. The researchers said this is the first case of AI reaching expert-level performance in live clinical video consultations. It was published on August 11, and the write-up was authored by Google senior research scientist Anil Palepu and research lead Mike Schaekermann.

AMIE (Video) runs a set of agents asynchronously. The Talker naturally carries the flow of conversation with the patient. The Planner runs clinical reasoning in the background, updating the differential diagnosis, while Perception reads clinically meaningful nonverbal cues from the audio and video stream. It's a structure that splits work needing an immediate response from work that needs deeper deliberation.

blocks.cap: An overview of AMIE for real-time clinical video consultations, the evaluation study, and key results.

blocks.x: The evaluation used 100 clinical scenarios spanning five body systems. It ran 300 standardized consultations, with 15 trained simulated patient actors taking part. There were three comparison arms: AMIE (Video), the text baseline AMIE (Text), and 10 primary care physicians.

blocks.cap: Diagnostic accuracy, clinical rater scores, and simulated patient actor preference for AMIE and primary care physician video visit quality.

blocks.x: In results scored by clinical raters, AMIE (Video) ran neck and neck with primary care physicians on core items like history-taking and diagnostic accuracy. It actually came out ahead on visual examination and guiding remote physical exams. Simulated patient actors clearly preferred AMIE on empathy and rapport.

blocks.cap: An ablation experiment comparing the video configuration with a text-chat-only configuration, based on clinical rater scores and simulated patient actor preference.

blocks.x: The researchers were clear about the limitations. They worked with professional actors rather than real patients, which narrowed the scope to conditions that could be reproduced through acting. Even with strong overall performance, there were cases of errors in perception and reasoning, and technical issues carried over from the Project Astra prototype stage remained.

Next is validation with real patients. The plan is to broaden the range of clinical presentations covered and pair it with ongoing real-world studies at partner institutions such as Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center and Included Health.

Researchers at Ca' Foscari University of Venice have introduced IceBoost v2.0, a machine learning model that maps the ice volume of the world's glaciers. Excluding Antarctica and Greenland, Earth's glaciers hold about 150,000 cubic kilometers of ice — enough to raise sea levels by 32.3 centimeters if it all melted.

blocks.cap: IceBoost v2.0 estimates global glacier ice volume at about 150,000 cubic kilometers.

blocks.x: The model was trained on more than 7 million field measurements of glacier thickness. It incorporated 26 physical and geometric variables, including terrain slope, ice flow velocity, and temperature. Lead researcher Niccolò Maffezzoli said the estimates match field observations up to 40% better.

"The distribution of glacier thickness is a fundamental variable for glaciology and climate models," said Maffezzoli, a physicist at Ca' Foscari University and a member of Italy's National Research Council Institute of Polar Sciences (CNR-ISP). To forecast how glaciers will change by 2100 and how much they'll add to sea levels, he said, you first need a fine-grained picture of their current state.
"Machine learning models open up a different path. Rather than imposing a predetermined physical description, they learn directly from the data to produce predictions," Maffezzoli explained.
A striking case is the Geikie Plateau in eastern Greenland. IceBoost v2.0 found nearly twice the ice previously reported there, with thickness reaching 2 kilometers in places.

The value comes from freshwater management. About 1.9 billion people worldwide depend on water that glaciers release. The model also points to where field observations should be prioritized going forward: the Himalaya, the Karakoram, and Patagonia's large ice fields.

"We need to move fast. We expect mid-latitude glaciers, including the Alps, to disappear within the coming decades," Maffezzoli said. The study was published in Scientific Data (DOI: 10.1038/s41597-026-07744-9) and is linked to the Glacier Model Intercomparison Project (GlacierMIP4). The results can be viewed directly through a web tool (https://nmaffe.github.io/iceboost_webapp/).

Last week OpenAI announced 10 math results produced with its next-generation large language model, Astra. The claim was that it had solved long-open problems, with total token costs coming to $2,000. But as mathematicians combed through the papers, citation concerns surfaced.

blocks.cap: Source: Malte Mueller/Getty Images

blocks.x: The first case is the sphere-packing problem, which deals with how to pack balls into mathematical spaces of more than 1,000 dimensions. Steven Miller of Yeshiva University believes Astra's solution reused the argument from a paper he co-authored in 2016, presenting it as if it were a new result.
"They're deliberately trampling over work by people who came before them. From where I stand, this is fully organized, and amounts to research misconduct," Miller said. He called it plagiarism.

The second case is group theory, a result claiming there's at least one group that lacks the property of soficity. Francesco Fournier-Facio of the University of Cambridge pointed out that the key idea here already appeared in papers from 2016 and 2019. Andreas Thom of TU Dresden, a co-author of the 2019 paper, also left a comment on MathOverflow.

Fournier-Facio isn't dismissing Astra's work itself. He described the result as "creative and elementary at the same time." But he believes what AI is good at is fitting puzzle pieces together, not making a genuinely new intellectual leap.

"There's a giant PR machine that wants this to sound impressive, and it isn't interested in whether it's 100% accurate," Fournier-Facio said. OpenAI's press release stated the problems had been open for "at least a decade" with no progress, but critics counter that there had been research done just before this.

An OpenAI spokesperson responded: "We take responsibility for the accuracy of these results and hold ourselves to the same standards generally expected of human mathematicians. In line with standard academic practice, we plan to make minor revisions to the paper this week."

The issue doesn't end with the plagiarism dispute alone. "OpenAI is now fully participating in top-tier research. If so, it should be held to the same academic standards as the rest of us," Fournier-Facio said. It's a demand that as AI takes a seat as a researcher, it should keep to the same norms of citation and sourcing. The article was written by Joseph Howlett and edited by Lee Billings.

Mathematicians tend to be cautious about new things. Even researchers armed with computers took years to transform the field as a whole. Now artificial intelligence, large language models in particular, is seeping into how mathematics gets done. Scientific American's Manon Bischoff met Yang-Hui He, a mathematician and physicist at the London Institute for Mathematical Sciences.

blocks.cap: A 3D illustration of a human head formed from geometric shapes. Source: Andriy Onufriyenko/Getty Images

blocks.x: He spent a long time working on string theory. The turn came in 2017. Instead of quantum gravity or the nature of time, everyone suddenly started talking about machine learning, and his own students began seeking machine learning jobs instead of positions in finance or academia. His son, born that year, wouldn't sleep, so He stayed up with him every night learning machine learning through online courses. Mathematica had just released a neural network framework, which was enough to start experimenting.

He applied that simple neural network to data on Calabi-Yau manifolds, the high-dimensional geometric objects at the heart of string theory. The experiment was meant to test whether it could recognize topological properties, and he didn't expect much. The network predicted certain properties with considerable accuracy. A machine that knew nothing about geometry or topology had learned a deep mathematical structure.

After the paper came out, several groups picked up similar ideas. He himself drifted away from string theory. Once he stripped away the physical motivation, he found himself using machines to explore the structure of mathematics itself.

Convincing physicists was easy. CERN had been using machine learning since at least the 1990s. Mathematicians were far more skeptical. 'For the past eight years I've felt like a traveling salesman,' he said. 'I'd move from field to field asking, do you have data, and shall we look together for hidden structure in it?' Since then he has worked with researchers in representation theory, algebraic geometry, number theory, combinatorics and differential geometry.

The most interesting effect of AI, He says, is a new shared language. Researchers in analytic number theory and experts in partial differential equations work in closely related fields yet speak different languages. But once they start talking about data, patterns and learning, a common ground suddenly appears. 'In that sense, AI strangely makes mathematics more human,' he said. 'It gets people talking to each other again.'

Pattern recognition and hypothesis generation were stage one. The next question is whether AI is actually useful for solving important unsolved problems. The evidence comes from FrontierMath, a project that creates new unsolved, difficult problems and solutions to measure AI capability. In the summer of 2025, He took part in tier 4, locked in a room with 30 mathematicians for several days to create problems. No one could leave so that conversations wouldn't leak onto the internet, and everyone signed non-disclosure agreements. AI cracked around 10% of the problem set within a month. Tier 5, which deals with meaningful unsolved problems, is now underway.

Asked what's left for humans if AI takes over the research, he said he isn't worried. He doesn't need to be the one proving a theorem; he just wants to know the answer. Interpretation, context and judgment remain human work. He compared it to Bach's music: you don't have to have composed it yourself to be moved listening to it all day, and mathematics can work the same way. You could even think of AI as the ultimate mathematics library. A colleague once asked a question about the Monster group so technical that even experts couldn't answer it right away, and a language model found the answer buried deep in an old paper's theorem. 'Even after people forget, AI will remember your research.'

A new AI chip mimics the instinctive motor responses of the human brain. Modeled on the cerebellum, which handles balance and fine muscle control, it's designed to let familiar information pass through and react only to unexpected events. In simulations using electrocardiogram (ECG) data, the device caught arrhythmias with 98% accuracy within one-fifth of a heartbeat. The research was published in Nature Communications on July 10.

blocks.cap: An illustration of a brain placed over an electronic circuit. The new chip works in a way similar to the human brain.

blocks.x: It could open a path toward low-power AI that notices and responds to anomalies without relying on the massive computation of data centers. The range of applications spans always-on health monitors to self-driving cars and robots. Computer architectures modeled on the human brain are called neuromorphic computing.

The brain's biological circuits don't process all incoming information with equal intensity. They prioritize important signals, filter out background noise and conserve energy. Neuromorphic research has generally targeted the cerebrum, the seat of thought. This research team chose the cerebellum instead.

blocks.cap: A map of the human brain, including the cerebellum.

blocks.x: In the cerebellum's neural circuits, competing excitatory and inhibitory signals maintain a balance. When something unexpected happens, that balance tips, telling the brain a response is needed. Co-author Mark Hersam, a professor of materials science and engineering at Northwestern University, says the cerebellum is an untapped candidate for neuromorphic AI. 'The cerebellum conserves its resources to ignore what's expected and respond to what's unexpected. That approach ultimately leads to lower energy consumption.'

Today's AI excels at pattern recognition but burns enormous amounts of computation constantly analyzing data streams. Hardware holds it back too: because memory and computation are handled by separate components, shuttling data between them creates a delay known as the von Neumann bottleneck. This device eliminates that back-and-forth by combining memory and computation into a single component called a memtransistor. It's built from atomically thin molybdenum disulfide semiconductor, with an asymmetric structure where only one electrode contacts the semiconductor directly, so reversing the voltage direction switches it between excitatory and inhibitory modes.

The device was designed to serve as the core of the output layer in a larger spiking neural network. The researchers measured the pulse response of a single memtransistor and used the results to simulate a network that distinguishes normal ECGs from arrhythmias. Feeding the same ECG data into both the cerebellum-inspired network and a standard transformer model and comparing detection speed and efficiency, the cerebellum-inspired version was more than twice as fast and used roughly 1/10,000th the computation.

Hersam said real-world performance depends on the device's speed and size, but that it leads to faster, more energy-efficient hardware. 'We haven't scaled it up to the level of commercial silicon chips, but in principle, 2D materials and memtransistors can be scaled to comparable sizes and operating speeds.' He added that it's especially well suited to settings like edge computing, where fast inference is needed with minimal power.

The bigger point is that this could shake up AI's reliance on data centers. The International Energy Agency projects global data center electricity demand will reach about 945 terawatt-hours by 2030, slightly more than Japan's total electricity consumption, with AI as the main driver. Hersam said, 'Our approach promises lower energy consumption by reducing the total amount of computation needed. It's not an incremental performance improvement but a fundamentally different way of doing anomaly detection.' The next step is to mimic the cerebellum's adaptive ability to stop treating a repeated event as special after encountering it multiple times.

Long before a dark sunspot appears on the Sun's surface, active regions, the sites where powerful solar eruptions begin, quietly leak signs of their formation. Researchers at the New Jersey Institute of Technology (NJIT) say they've built an AI model that reads those early signals to forecast the emergence of active regions nearly nine hours ahead, on average.

In a paper published in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Machine Learning and Computation, the researchers report that a model called EarlyDetect picks up precursors of active region emergence in the Sun's acoustic activity and magnetic field. The corresponding author is Jonas Tirona, an undergraduate researcher at NJIT. Researchers from NJIT, Princeton University and NASA's Ames Research Center worked together using data from NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory (SDO).

blocks.cap: Source: Unsplash/CC0 Public Domain

blocks.x: 'The most valuable thing this study shows is that machine learning can predict in advance when solar active regions will appear,' said Tirona, a computer science major entering his senior year. 'With that early warning, satellite communication companies or power grid operators can prepare and reduce the damage from solar storms.'

Active regions, the magnetically strong areas where sunspots form, emerge over the course of several hours. As the magnetic field rises to the surface, it leaves a faint trace in sound waves, a mark that helioseismology, the study of the Sun's oscillations, can pick up. EarlyDetect reads hourly maps of acoustic power and magnetic field measurements from SDO.

'The hardest part is that active regions start growing beneath the Sun's visible surface, where the magnetic structure can't be observed directly,' explained Alexander Kosovichev, distinguished professor of physics at NJIT and project co-lead. 'It's a bit like noticing a slightly off beat inside an extremely noisy orchestra.'

The model's backbone is a transformer, the same architecture used by large language models like ChatGPT. Tirona, who joined the team last year, and the rest of the team found something unexpected: filtering added to highlight important patterns was actually ruining the forecasts. Kosovichev said that was the biggest surprise. 'We expected it to isolate useful short-term patterns, but instead it averaged away the faint fluctuations that gave the earliest warnings.' Tirona said, 'The signal the filter stripped out turned out to be really important for predicting when an active region would emerge.'

After training on SDO/HMI observations, the team tested the model on active regions it had never seen before. The best-performing version caught precursors an average of 9.24 hours before the active region became visible, outperforming both a standard transformer model and existing benchmark methods. Mengjia Xu, project lead and assistant professor of data science at NJIT, said the study shows that advanced machine learning models open new possibilities for space weather forecasting. The team also released a public dataset called SolARED.

That said, it's not yet ready for real-time forecasting. Because it was trained on known emergence events, it still produces false alarms and sometimes predicts late. A warning that an active region is emerging also doesn't predict a flare or coronal mass ejection. Tirona said, 'It would be really cool if models like this could one day help predict space weather. We're not there yet, but it's an exciting step.'

Some people find that saying a hard problem out loud helps them think it through. But cognitive neuroscientists at MIT's McGovern Institute for Brain Research believe language itself isn't necessary for logical reasoning. In a study published in PNAS, a team led by Evelina Fedorenko, an associate professor of brain and cognitive sciences at MIT, confirmed that even people whose language abilities are severely impaired can solve logical reasoning problems. Brain imaging also showed that language-processing regions weren't recruited for logical reasoning.

blocks.cap: A functional brain scan of a neurotypical participant. Activity for logic (green) and language (red/yellow) is clearly separated. Source: Hope Kean, MIT

blocks.x: Philosophers, linguists and cognitive scientists have argued for thousands of years over whether language is essential to thought. Many have viewed language as the tool of thinking. Hope Kean, a postdoctoral researcher in Fedorenko's lab, says there's good reason for that view. 'Abstract thought shares a lot of properties with language. You can break thoughts into small atoms, logical propositions, and combine them hierarchically to build more complex rules.' Still, the two suspected that the brain separates the communication of reasoning from reasoning itself. Logical reasoning demands a precision that everyday language doesn't offer, and unlike language, which flows linearly word by word, the path to a conclusion is less linear.

Verification was tricky, since explaining the task to participants and getting their answers both depend on language. Fedorenko's team partnered with Rosemary Varley's team at University College London, which studies acquired language impairment. The subjects were two people whose language regions were damaged by stroke, leaving them with severe difficulty understanding and producing speech. To bypass language, the researchers built logic games using numbers and visual patterns: a task of finding the hidden rule that reverses one list of numbers into another and applying it to new examples, and a task of choosing which geometric pattern correctly completes a matrix.

The result held even as the puzzles got harder. Participants with severe language impairment solved them as well as the control group, and even conveyed the rules they'd discovered through gestures or drawings. Kean said the result 'directly overturns the theory that symbolic rule induction is impossible without language ability.'

The team also examined the brains of healthy adults. Participants underwent multiple MRI sessions at MIT, performing logic games, tasks that mapped each person's own language-processing regions, and tasks that mapped the 'multiple demand network' that supports complex problem-solving. They also solved syllogisms like, 'If a ball is red, then it is big. The ball is red. Is the ball big?' The scans were unambiguous: the language system didn't switch on either for induction, finding hidden rules, or for deduction, assessing the validity of syllogisms. The surprise was the multiple demand network, which activated for induction but didn't participate in deduction.

The two researchers read this as evidence that language and logic rest on separate systems in the brain. Professionals who work with people with aphasia have long known that losing language isn't losing intelligence. Fedorenko said, 'A growing body of research shows that abstract logical thinking is preserved even with severe aphasia,' stressing that language difficulty says nothing about a person's intelligence or ability.

There are implications for artificial intelligence too. Large language models like ChatGPT and Claude are trained entirely on text and produce text, yet plausibly mimic human reasoning. The human brain works differently. Kean believes that examining how human reasoning diverges from the way language models operate can offer clues for future AI design.

When an LLM gets a fact wrong, did it never learn it, or did it learn it but fail to retrieve it? The knowledge-profiling framework that Google Research scientists Nitay Calderon and Gal Yona released on August 12 points to the latter. A single accuracy metric blurs the two cases together, but the fixes differ completely. A storage failure calls for bigger models and more data; a retrieval failure calls for post-training and inference-time techniques.

blocks.cap: The five knowledge profiles that divide the state of a fact.

blocks.x: The researchers split storing a fact in the parameters into encoding, pulling it out without external cues into recall, and picking the right answer from options into recognition. They also moved the unit of analysis from questions to facts themselves. Each fact is classified as an encoding failure, a recall failure, direct retrieval, retrieval through reasoning, or inference without encoding.

To measure this, the team built the WikiProfile benchmark from 2,150 facts drawn from Wikipedia. Each fact carries ten tasks: two for encoding, four for knowledge assessment, and four multiple-choice. Construction was handled by Gemini-2.5-Pro with thinking turned on, followed by search-engine-based filtering and a final manual check. The team evaluated 13 LLMs with thinking on and off, collecting roughly 4.5 million responses.

blocks.cap: The five-profile distribution across 13 LLMs. Encoding failures drop sharply with scale, but recall failures persist.

blocks.x: In Gemini-2.5-Pro, Gemini-3-Pro/Flash, and GPT-5, encoding has nearly saturated. Gemini-3-Pro and GPT-5 encoded 95-98% of facts yet failed to retrieve 26-34% of them directly, and even with thinking turned on, 11-12% were still wrong. The bottleneck has shifted from storing knowledge to using it. In the Gemma 3 family too, scaling up sharply cuts encoding failures, but recall failures make up an even larger share of the errors that remain.

blocks.cap: Encoding and direct-retrieval rates for the bottom 20% and top 20% of facts by popularity. The gap is narrow in encoding and wide in retrieval.

blocks.x: Retrieval is tied to the conditions under which a fact was learned. The further a question strays from the context, phrasing, or order it was learned in, the harder it is to pull out. Rare facts are encoded at rates similar to popular ones, yet the gap opens wide only in retrieval. The long-tail problem turns out to be about access, not capacity. Reversed questions follow the same pattern: asked as multiple choice, the reverse direction is actually easier, but asked as direct generation, it gets harder. The reversal curse is a retrieval problem.

blocks.cap: The share of facts newly recovered when thinking is turned on. 40-65% of encoded facts are recovered, versus just 5-15% of unencoded facts.

blocks.x: Thinking helps most exactly where direct retrieval is weakest. In models optimized for thinking, 40-65% of facts that were encoded but not immediately known were recovered, versus just 5-15% for facts that were never encoded. That suggests thinking opens a path to facts already stored, rather than constructing answers through multi-step reasoning. But thinking carries a compute cost, and when to turn it on remains an open question.

Google DeepMind unveiled SL2T, a translation model that converts sign language into text, on August 12. It is the first time sign-language AI has moved out of the lab and into a consumer product. The feature that translates American Sign Language (ASL) into English launches first in Gboard and Live Transcribe on the Pixel 11, with supported devices and languages set to expand gradually.

blocks.cap: Gboard's sign-language dictation, used to type in sign language while holding the phone with one hand.

blocks.x: Just as hearing users dictate by voice, deaf users can now input in sign language right where they used to type. That covers web searches, messages, documents, and even asking Gemini to do tasks. In Live Transcribe, they can simply sign a reply instead of exchanging text. Testers said signing in ASL felt faster, more natural, and more enjoyable than typing in English.

Sign language isn't English mapped onto the hands. More than 200 sign languages worldwide are independent natural languages with their own grammar and vocabulary, so they need genuine machine translation rather than swapping words one by one. Meaning is made by the hands, arms, torso, head, and face moving together, which also places a heavy computer-vision burden on tracking all of that at a high frame rate. That is why early attempts like sign-language gloves hit a wall.

SL2T was trained on more than 100,000 hours of data gathered from over 50 sign languages, about a quarter of it ASL. Training on a mix of languages, dialects, and skill levels together let the model learn shared structure and outperform single-language models. Privacy is protected by design: only the pose coordinates extracted on-device by MediaPipe Holistic are sent to the server, and the original video is discarded immediately.

SL2T also skips the intermediate gloss notation that earlier research relied on, since gloss cannot capture nuances like non-manual signals and spatial structure. By converting the coordinate sequence straight into text, it removes vocabulary limits and lets translation quality scale with the amount of data. On FLEURS-ASL (sd-test), which measures ASL-English translation, SL2T scored 70 BLEURT zero-shot. The team also tackled real-world challenges such as cutting streaming latency, blocking hallucinations on non-sign input, and handling the 10% of signers who are left-handed as well as one-handed signing.

The project ran on the principle of building with the deaf community, not just for it. It began with an idea from Sam Sepah, a deaf Google employee, and the community's perspective was built into every stage, from data collection to user research to impact assessment. For responsible deployment, the team formed the AI Sign Language Advisory Council (AISLAC), bringing together deaf organizations and experts worldwide, and released a joint impact report detailing the features and limits of SL2T alongside the 1.0 launch.
The team plans to add more sign languages and expand into sign-language generation and frontier AI features. SL2T is available at no extra cost in Gboard and Live Transcribe on the Pixel 11.

Vivodyne announced that it has opened what it calls the “world's largest human biology datacenter.” Across 12 robotic labs called HIVE, it runs controlled trials every year on 3.1 million large human tissues. The company estimates this scale at roughly twice the combined total of every clinical trial running in the United States.

blocks.cap: Rows of automated human-tissue testing equipment inside Vivodyne's Human Datacenter. [Vivodyne]

blocks.x: Launched alongside it, the Series 2 TissueDisk is a wafer-sized biology chip. It grows hundreds of functioning large human tissues simultaneously and is built start to finish on Vivodyne's own robotic production line. Eight of the world's largest pharmaceutical companies have already paid for early access to the platform.

Co-founder and CEO Andrei Georgescu says that together, TissueDisk and the HIVE labs create an experimental environment that neither pharmaceutical research nor AI has ever had. The scale is large enough, he says, to apply the reinforcement-learning techniques that grew language models to human physiology itself. For drugmakers, it means seeing how real human tissue responds while targets, chemical structures, dosage, and safety can still be changed. Millions of therapeutic interventions are applied to living human tissue, with causal outcomes measured directly through 3D scanning, transcriptomic sequencing, and deep proteomics.

blocks.cap: Vivodyne began as an idea Andrei Georgescu (left, now CEO) had while pursuing his Ph.D. in the bioengineering lab of UPenn professor Dan Huh (right, now CSO). [Penn Engineering]

blocks.x: “Superintelligence in biology is needed now more than ever, because we're running out of diseases that today's simple, single-target drugs can fix,” Georgescu said. “You can't fix a car by turning one screw. The idea that the complex breakdowns behind cancer, fibrosis, autoimmune disease, and neurological disease can be fixed with a conventional single-target drug is wishful denial.” Since you can't put people at risk to get the data, the approach instead grows millions of large human tissues that build their own blood vessels and immune cells. That tissue grows, gets sick, bleeds, and scars.

Vivodyne grows more than 20 types of human organ tissue, including liver, lung, intestine, bone marrow, pancreas, kidney, eye, and lymph node, in both healthy states and patient-derived disease states. It also has disease-specific versions covering fibrosis, site-specific solid tumors, inflammation, metabolic disease, and vascular disease. The experiments accumulated for each organ train causal multimodal models, and the idea is that linking those models across organ systems adds up to a world model of the human body.

That model answers what happens when a drug engages a given pair of receptors, what follows when a biological pathway is cut, and why an unexpected side effect arises. Its predictions are then refined by validating them at scale back in human tissue.

A new AI system cuts robot response latency by more than 10x without any extra computation. Robots driven by vision-language-action (VLA) models tend to move in stops and starts: reach, pause, adjust, pause again. That is because of how they run, finishing one batch of instructions and then waiting for the next batch to be computed. This latency has made VLA robots hard to use for tasks that require continuous real-time interaction.

VLASH removes that wait by planning the next move while the current one is still being carried out. In experiments, robots using VLASH finished some tasks 1.5-2x faster while keeping most or all of their accuracy. Maximum response latency dropped by up to 11.8x, depending on the hardware used.

Researchers from MIT, NVIDIA, Caltech, UC Berkeley, UC San Diego, and China's Tsinghua University posted the paper on arXiv and will present it at the International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems this fall. An earlier version of the paper listed a speedup of more than 30x, but the researchers told Live Science that those experiments used longer action sequences and slower hardware. They explained that the 11.8x figure may better reflect current real-world conditions.

A VLA model combines camera images, human instructions, and the robot's current state and turns them into actual movement. While the robot is finishing a batch of motion, VLASH estimates the ending point from its current position and planned motion, then plans the next batch from that predicted state. Rather than waiting for a foot to touch the ground before deciding the next step, it decides in advance, before the foot lands. Unlike a world model that renders the entire surrounding environment, VLASH predicts only the robot itself. Because it draws future states from motion that is already planned, it needs no separate prediction model and no extra inference step at execution time.

The researchers tested two VLA models and two robot platforms on a laptop equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. They ran pick-and-place, stacking, and sorting tasks 20 times each for every method, and added fast-reaction tasks like table tennis and whack-a-mole. In those two tasks, the target moves while the robot is still computing. Rather than predicting that movement, VLASH processes 15-30 new observations per second, letting it quickly catch changes such as an object being moved.

Speed isn't the same as safety. Roshni Lulla, co-founder and chief research officer of the Human-Centered Robotics Lab, who was not involved in the research, said, “Being more responsive is a clear benefit, but I'm not sure there's evidence that safety has improved.” She said it should be tested in a room with people present, where another agent is changing the environment. Lulla summed up the results narrowly: a processing-time bottleneck was removed while existing performance was preserved.

AI produces solutions that people would rarely think of. What if machines went beyond solving individual problems and discovered entirely new strategies? Could such discoveries become part of human knowledge?

The Center for Humans and Machines at the Max Planck Institute for Human Development, together with researchers from the Toulouse School of Economics and Humboldt University of Berlin, put this question to the test for the first time. According to results published in Nature Communications, under certain conditions people accepted strategies discovered by machines and passed them down and preserved them across generations.

blocks.cap: A machine's strategy becomes human culture. Credit: MPI for Human Development

blocks.x: The study began with the observation that AI keeps producing strategies that surprise experts, as seen when it found unfamiliar yet powerful moves in Go and chess. But the conditions under which such discoveries would endure in human thinking and behavior were unclear.

The researchers identified three conditions: a strategy must be hard to discover at first, yet learnable, and its advantage must be clearly visible. Only then can it spread through a community and persist over time.

Lead author Levin Brinkmann, a researcher at the Center for Humans and Machines, said, “Human cultural evolution relies on knowledge being passed down through countless individuals and generations. The question now is whether a strategy discovered by a machine can also become part of that inherited knowledge. That is exactly what we looked at.”

1,155 people took part in the experiment. The goal was to score as many points as possible in a task with a specially designed reward structure. The optimal strategy required accepting a small loss early on to gain a much larger payoff later, which ran directly against people's instinct to avoid short-term losses at all costs.

Participants were grouped into chains that learned from each other across generations. Some groups were made up only of humans, while others included AI agents from the start. These agents had already found the optimal strategy by solving the task with a learning algorithm beforehand. Participants could see and reference the successful solutions of the previous generation.

The result was clear. The optimal strategy almost never emerged in groups without AI; among 600 people, only one found the best solution on their own. In groups that included AI, by contrast, the machine-discovered strategy spread frequently and survived across generations. In nine of 15 mixed human-machine groups, the strategy remained in use throughout the experiment.

Participants showed a clear tendency to follow the most successful examples. Most modeled their behavior on whichever person or agent had the best score, which is how the machine's strategy spread and persisted.

Co-lead author Thomas Eisenmann, also a researcher at the center, said, “There is a lot of debate over whether AI makes people more dependent. Our results point to a different possibility: if people can understand a machine's discovery, they learn new abilities, retain them over time, and expand their cultural repertoire.”

This study adds empirical evidence to the concept of “machine culture.” Much of AI's current capability comes from machines learning human knowledge and culture, as with large language models trained on vast amounts of human writing. This result shows that the flow is not one-way: people, too, build their abilities on machine discoveries. It is an era of machine culture, in which humans and machines are bound into a single cultural evolutionary process and become sources of innovation for each other.

blocks.cap: A photonic microchip is about the size of a coin. It shows computer-designed nanostructures, including a wavelength splitter, a mode sorter, and a mirror.

blocks.x: Three components used in photonic microchips have been shrunk by up to 500 times. The shrinking was done not by people but by an AI algorithm that solves the design problem in reverse, and the researchers described the results as going “beyond human intuition.” The extra space freed up means the chip can carry more functions.

Unlike ordinary chips that use electrons, photonic chips carry information using particles of light. Because signals travel at the speed of light, processing and transmission are fast, and different wavelengths can carry different data, giving wide bandwidth. Less energy leaks out as heat as well. That is why they are used wherever fast, high-volume transmission is needed, such as fiber-optic communication, data centers, AI, autonomous-driving lidar, and quantum computing.

Inside the chip, instead of metal wiring, waveguides just a few micrometers wide carry the light. The wavelength splitter, spatial mode sorter, and mirror separate wavelengths and light patterns and steer their direction within an area that is only a fraction of the width of a human hair. The researchers made these three components ultra-small, and the results were published in Nature Communications on May 28.

The method works like this: the algorithm is first told how the light should behave, along with manufacturing constraints such as how sharply a nanostructure can bend. The algorithm then works backward, testing and refining designs until it finds a delicate nanostructure that produces the desired result.

Toby Bi, the paper's first author and a researcher at the Max Planck Institute for the Science of Light, said, “In inverse design, we define what we want the light to do, and optimization finds the structure that does it. Often it's a structure a human would never have drawn.” It is also notable that the same framework performs three jobs on one chip: splitting light by wavelength, sorting it by spatial mode, and acting as the small mirror that forms an on-chip optical resonator.

blocks.cap: The component shape refined by the AI algorithm through iterative optimization.

blocks.x: Photonic chip components are usually designed by hand, starting from a proven layout and painstakingly refining it to fit new performance requirements. This approach is slow, and the range of shapes that can be tried is narrow.

The researchers chose a relatively thick silicon nitride for the components. At 400 to 800 nanometers thick, versus 150 to 400 nanometers for standard silicon, it loses less light and confines wavelengths more tightly. A mirror just over 11 μm long reflected up to 98.5 percent of incoming light, and when paired on either side of a waveguide, light bounced more than 100 times before escaping. The wavelength splitter is about 5 μm, roughly the size of a single bacterium, and the spatial mode sorter is a bit larger.

The three components have not yet been combined into a single photonic integrated circuit. That step must still be taken for a complete photonic chip that takes advantage of the higher density to emerge. The researchers wrote in the paper, “These results show that small, fabrication-tolerant, and customizable optical components are achievable.”

Efforts to weave AI into semiconductor design and manufacturing have surged in recent years. Some cases have cut design cycles from weeks to hours and sharply lowered manufacturing costs, and there are systems that can produce usable chip designs from just a 200-word prompt. Google's AlphaChip produced a layout described as “superhuman” and went into actual production of the company's AI chips.

blocks.x: The boldest promise the AI industry makes today is recursive self-improvement: the idea that AI will soon improve itself with little human involvement. Already, LLMs write code, generate synthetic training data, and optimize the chips they run on.

A new study suggests that moment is further off than it seems. The researchers confirmed that AI agents still cannot carry out open-ended AI research — free-form inquiry without a predetermined answer that requires judgment and discernment.

A multi-institution team led by Peter Kirgis and Sayash Kapoor of Princeton University found that agents can solve the engineering problems AI research requires, but lack the judgment and creativity to produce original work worthy of top machine learning conferences. It's a sign that optimistic timelines for automating AI research have outrun the evidence.

Existing evaluations mostly dealt with narrow tasks whose answers could be checked. The researchers instead proposed “shadow evaluation,” posing an AI with the exact research question from a strong paper that had not yet been published. The targets were two papers submitted to NeurIPS 2026. One asked whether weight editing could control the “personas” that govern a model's behavior; the other asked for a detector that could catch when a model predicting from tabular data loses reliability. Because the papers weren't public yet, there was no way to memorize or search for the answers.

The experiment used Anthropic's Claude Opus 4.8 running on the open-source software OpenClaw. Each agent was given six days, $3,000 in Anthropic API credits, a GPU budget, its own virtual computer, and web access. The original papers' authors graded the work themselves, as if reviewing for a conference.

The engineering was fine. The agents surveyed the literature, ran hundreds of experiments, and organized results. “But they were clearly bad at doing the research itself,” Kapoor says. They ran bizarre experiments, such as testing hypotheses on tiny amounts of synthetic data, failed to write up their own work clearly, and left no new contribution behind.

What held them back was creativity and judgment. They didn't explore enough ideas before latching onto a hopeless approach too quickly. They came up with ambitious hypotheses similar to what the original authors had first proposed, then abandoned them on their own after seeing only weak data. They couldn't back out of failed paths or restructure their approach. There was no reward hacking — no hiding or distorting results.
There are limits to the study. It covered only two papers, and the graders knew the work came from AI. The researchers are now running the same experiment with Anthropic's newest model, Mythos.

Anthropic cofounder Jack Clark wrote in his newsletter Import AI that “today's AI systems have a consistent lack of valuable, intuitive creativity, and can be extremely capable engineers while still having mechanical, formulaic thinking habits that may make it hard for them to be good researchers.” He called it a “bearish signal” for short timelines to recursive self-improvement.

Kapoor sums up the remaining question this way: “Like the invention of the transformer, every major advance in this field has required a creative leap.” Whether grinding through narrow tasks alone can still reach self-improvement is, he says, “the trillion-dollar question right now.”
